topic.title: Interval Estimation
topic.summary: Covers generating narrow confidence intervals (confidence limits) that enclose an unknown parameter with a high probability. Assuming a normal population, it walks through deriving and computing 100(1-alpha)% confidence intervals for the population mean (mu) and variance (sigma squared) under different scenarios: when sigma squared is known or unknown, and when mu is known or unknown.
subtopics: 100(1-alpha)% confidence intervals for the population mean (mu)
100(1-alpha)% confidence intervals for the population variance (sigma squared)
Cases when sigma squared is known or unknown
Cases when mu is known or unknown

evidence_quotes: Introduces the concept of parameter estimation using sample characteristics or statistics, distinguishing population characteristics (parameters, which are usually unknown) from sample characteristics (statistics, which are usually known).
Outlines the four properties of a "best" estimator according to R.A. Fisher: unbiasedness, consistency, efficiency, and sufficiency.
Covers generating narrow confidence intervals (confidence limits) that enclose an unknown parameter with a high probability.

LESSON ONE
 CONCEPT OF ESTIMATION

 1.1 Introduction

 In this lesson we introduce the concept of estimation and distinguishing between parameters
 and statistics. Two types of methods of estimation will also be discussed.

 1.2 Learning Outcomes

 By the end of this lesson the learner will be able to:

 1.2.1 Explain the concept of estimation of parameters using sample characteristics
 or statistics.
 1.2.2 Distinguish between point and interval estimations
 1.2.1 Concept of Estimation

 The objective of statistics is to make an inference about a population based on information

 contained in a sample. Most statistical inference procedures involve either estimation or
 hypothesis testing. This course looks at estimation.

 1.2.2 Point and Interval Estimations
 (i) Point Estimation
 A point estimation procedure utilizes the sample information to arrive at a single number or
 point that estimates the population parameter.
 If we let the value of some statistic say t(X 1, X 2, …Xn ) to estimate the unknown parameter,
 then t(X 1, X 2, …Xn ) is called a point estimator.
 (ii) Interval Estimation
 An interval estimation procedure makes use of the sample information to arrive at two
 numbers that are intended to enclose the parameter of interest.
 This is where two statistics t 1 (X 1, X 2, …Xn ) and t 2 (X 1, X 2, …Xn ) where t 1 (X 1, X 2, …Xn ) < t 2 (X 1,
 X 2, …Xn ) so that [t 1 (X 1, X 2, …Xn ), t 2 (X 1, X 2, …Xn )] constitutes an interval for which the
 probability can be determined that it contains the unknown parameter.
 In either case, the actual estimation is accomplished by an estimator. An estimator is a rule
 or formula that tells us how to calculate an estimate based on measurements contained in a
 sample. Most frequently, an estimator is expressed as a formula.

LESSON THREE

 Sufficiency and efficiency of an estimators

 3.1 Introduction

 This lesson looks at the sufficiency and efficiency properties of a good estimator.

 3.2 Learning Outcomes
 By the end of this lesson the learner will be able to:

 1.2.1 Define sufficiency and test whether an estimator is sufficient or not.
 1.2.2 Define efficiency and test whether an estimator is efficient or not
 3.2.1 Sufficiency

 Definition

 Let X 1, X 2, …Xn be a random sample of size n from a population having a random variable X

 whose pdf is of the form f(x,)which is known except the parameter is unknown. The
 statistic T=t(X 1, X 2, …Xn ) is said to be a sufficient statistics for if the conditional

 distribution of X given t does not depend on.

 That is if P(X=x/T=t) is independent of the parameter, then T is a sufficient statistic for the

 parameter.

 A statistic is said to be sufficient for  if it carries all information about  that is carried by

 the sample. We require an estimator to carry all information about whatever it is estimating

 that is originally contained in the sample. Intuitively, we would wish the estimator to carry
 all the relevant information in the sample regarding the parameter. That is it should be

 sufficient.

current_level_2_content:
## 1. Confidence limits and normal samples

An interval estimator gives lower and upper confidence limits for an unknown parameter. For a normal population, exact intervals can be derived from pivots with normal, Student t, or chi-square distributions. A $100(1-alpha)%$ procedure has that long-run coverage when the sampling model and the stated known/unknown parameter conditions hold.

Use $Xbar$ for the sample mean and $S^2=(n-1)^(-1)sum_i(X_i-Xbar)^2$ for the unbiased sample variance. Keep the degrees of freedom tied to whether the population mean is known or estimated.

## 2. Confidence interval for the population mean

If $X_i$ are independent normal observations with known population variance $sigma^2$, then $(Xbar-mu)/(sigma/sqrt(n))$ is standard normal. The two-sided interval is $Xbar +/- z_(1-alpha/2)sigma/sqrt(n)$.

If $sigma^2$ is unknown, replace $sigma$ by $S$. For a normal population, $(Xbar-mu)/(S/sqrt(n))$ follows a t distribution with $n-1$ degrees of freedom, giving $Xbar +/- t_(1-alpha/2,n-1)S/sqrt(n)$. The t formula is exact under normality; the known-variance z formula should not silently substitute $S$ in a small sample.

## 3. Confidence interval for population variance

For a normal sample with unknown mean, $(n-1)S^2/sigma^2$ follows chi-square with $n-1$ degrees of freedom. If $chi^2_(q,nu)$ denotes the q quantile with $nu$ degrees of freedom, the two-sided interval for $sigma^2$ is $[(n-1)S^2/chi^2_(1-alpha/2,n-1), (n-1)S^2/chi^2_(alpha/2,n-1)]$. The reversed quantile placement is necessary because the pivot is in the denominator.

If the population mean $mu$ is known, use $Q=sum_i(X_i-mu)^2$ and $Q/sigma^2~chi^2_n$. The interval becomes $[Q/chi^2_(1-alpha/2,n), Q/chi^2_(alpha/2,n)]$. This known-mean case has $n$ degrees of freedom; estimating the mean costs one degree of freedom.

## 4. Choosing the correct case

For an interval for $mu$, determine whether $sigma$ is known: use z when it is known and t with $n-1$ degrees of freedom when it is estimated from a normal sample. For an interval for $sigma^2$, determine whether $mu$ is known: center the squared deviations at the known $mu$ for $n$ degrees of freedom, or at $Xbar$ for $n-1$ degrees of freedom.

Intervals for variance are generally asymmetric. If the question asks for a confidence interval for standard deviation, take square roots of both positive variance endpoints. Do not use the normal-theory chi-square interval without the normal population assumption.

## 5. Calculation checklist

Write the target parameter and known quantities first. Select the pivot, confidence-tail probabilities, and degrees of freedom; obtain the matching critical values; then isolate the parameter carefully. For a variance interval, place the larger chi-square quantile in the denominator of the lower endpoint.

Check that variance endpoints are positive and ordered, that units are squared for $sigma^2$, and that the result is in the original units if square roots are requested. Explain the confidence level as repeated-sample coverage, not as a probability assigned to a fixed parameter after the interval is observed.

relevant_verified_questions.question: A random sample of $n=25$ steel rods from a normal population has a sample mean diameter of $\bar{x}=10.02$ mm. The population standard deviation is known to be $\sigma=0.05$ mm. Construct a $95\%$ confidence interval for the population mean diameter $\mu$.
relevant_verified_questions.solution:
Since the population is normal and $\sigma$ is known, the $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval for $\mu$ is

$$
\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

Here $1-\alpha=0.95$, so $\alpha=0.05$ and $z_{0.025}=1.96$. Given $\bar{x}=10.02$, $\sigma=0.05$, and $n=25$, the standard error is

$$
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}=\frac{0.05}{\sqrt{25}}=0.01.
$$

The margin of error is

$$
z_{0.025}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}=1.96(0.01)=0.0196.
$$

Thus the $95\%$ confidence interval is

$$
10.02 \pm 0.0196 = (10.0004,\, 10.0396).
$$

We are $95\%$ confident that the true mean diameter lies between $10.0004$ mm and $10.0396$ mm.

relevant_verified_questions.question:
A random sample of 12 fuel rods from a normal population gave the following summary statistics on percentage enrichment:

$$
\sum_{i=1}^{12} x_i = 34.82, \qquad \sum_{i=1}^{12} x_i^2 = 101.1486.
$$

Construct a \(99\%\) confidence interval for the population mean percentage enrichment \(\mu\). Assume the measurements are normally distributed with unknown variance \(\sigma^2\).
relevant_verified_questions.solution:
Let \(n=12\). The sample mean is

$$
\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i=\frac{34.82}{12}=2.901666\ldots \approx 2.9017.
$$

The sample variance is

$$
s^2=\frac{1}{n-1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i^2-\frac{(\sum x_i)^2}{n}\right)
=\frac{1}{11}\left(101.1486-\frac{(34.82)^2}{12}\right).
$$

Compute

$$
\frac{(34.82)^2}{12}=\frac{1212.4324}{12}=101.036033\ldots,
$$

so

$$
s^2=\frac{101.1486-101.036033\ldots}{11}
=\frac{0.112566\ldots}{11}
=0.010233\ldots.
$$

Thus \(s=\sqrt{0.010233\ldots}\approx 0.10116\).

Since \(\sigma^2\) is unknown and the population is normal, use the \(t\)-distribution with \(n-1=11\) degrees of freedom. For a \(99\%\) confidence interval, \(\alpha=0.01\), so we need \(t_{0.005,11}\). From \(t\)-tables,

$$
t_{0.005,11}\approx 3.106.
$$

The standard error is

$$
\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}=\frac{0.10116}{\sqrt{12}}\approx \frac{0.10116}{3.4641}\approx 0.02920.
$$

The margin of error is

$$
E=t_{0.005,11}\cdot \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\approx 3.106\times 0.02920\approx 0.0907.
$$

Therefore the \(99\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) is

$$
\bar{x}\pm E \approx 2.9017\pm 0.0907,
$$

that is,

$$
(2.8110,\;2.9924).
$$

So we are \(99\%\) confident that the true mean percentage enrichment lies between approximately \(2.81\%\) and \(2.99\%\).

relevant_verified_questions.question: A random sample of 10 children from a certain population was taken and their weights (in kg) were recorded. The sample mean weight was found to be \(38.4\text{ kg}\). Assume that the population of weights is normally distributed with unknown mean \(\mu\) and known variance \(\sigma^2 = 30\text{ kg}^2\). Construct a \(98\%\) confidence interval for the population mean weight \(\mu\).
relevant_verified_questions.solution:
Let \(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_{10}\) be the weights of the 10 children. We assume \(X_i \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\) with \(\sigma^2 = 30\) known. The sample mean is \(\bar{x} = 38.4\). The sample size is \(n = 10\).

For a \(100(1-\alpha)\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) when \(\sigma^2\) is known, we use the pivot

$$
Z = \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \sim N(0,1).
$$

Thus

$$
P\left(-z_{\alpha/2} \le \frac{\bar{X} - \mu}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}} \le z_{\alpha/2}\right) = 1-\alpha,
$$

which gives the confidence interval

$$
\bar{x} \pm z_{\alpha/2} \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}.
$$

Here \(1-\alpha = 0.98\), so \(\alpha = 0.02\) and \(\alpha/2 = 0.01\). From the standard normal table, \(z_{0.01} \approx 2.326\).

The standard error is

$$
\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} = \frac{\sqrt{30}}{\sqrt{10}} = \sqrt{3} \approx 1.732.
$$

The margin of error is

$$
z_{0.01} \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}} \approx 2.326 \times 1.732 \approx 4.028.
$$

Therefore, the \(98\%\) confidence interval for \(\mu\) is

$$
38.4 \pm 4.028 = (34.372,\; 42.428).
$$

So we are \(98\%\) confident that the true mean weight of the children lies between approximately \(34.37\text{ kg}\) and \(42.43\text{ kg}\).
